10:20 local Time, 09:20 GMT, 14:50 IST: Joe Root’s return as England captain could hardly have got off to a better start. He won the toss, opted to bowl first and hoped his bowlers could make the most of the overcast conditions - and exploit them they did. Ollie Robinson set the tone by striking with the very first ball of the game, before Josh Tongue removed the other opener, Imam-ul-Haq, to open the floodgates. Pakistan were eventually bowled out for just 171 inside 49 overs, with Robinson and Tongue claiming five wickets apiece. England lost both openers in quick succession in reply, but Root and Jordan Cox steadied things with a proactive 64-run stand to round off an excellent opening day for the hosts.

10:25 local, 09:25 GMT, 14:55 IST: It may have been a dream start for Root yesterday, but Day 2 has begun on a rather different note. While we wait for some positive news on the weather front, here’s something to keep you company. England skipper Joe Root spoke to Sky Sports’ Michael Atherton in Cardiff last week, touching on a range of interesting topics and offering some insight into his thoughts on the game, his captaincy and plenty more...

Joe Root: (Asked whether anything during the Oval Test against New Zealand changed his mind about taking the captaincy again) No, but as you mentioned, there was a lot to contend with that week for everyone involved and all the players, and I think when you find yourself in amongst chaos, you do learn a lot about each other. And I thought the way that the lads handled themselves around the game was exceptional. And I wouldn't say anything put me off throughout that week. There was a lot of changes and a lot of differences with everyone to contend with, and we just didn't manage certain elements of the game as well as we might have. And some of that was down to inexperience, some of that was down to the quality of New Zealand as well, and us not being able to respond to that. And I think they're all lessons that you take on board, both personally and collectively, so that you're better for it if you find yourself there again down the line.

Joe Root: (On whether he was disappointed that Brendan McCullum's tenure as Test coach ended after just one game) Yeah. I mean, I'll be honest with you, I was gutted when I found out Brendan was no longer going to be the Test coach. He's someone that I feel has really got the best out of me personally. I've loved the way he sees the game and the way that he's opened my eyes up to looking at it slightly differently, even after 120-odd games or whatever it was by the time he took over. So I feel like he's a brilliant coach. I'm very glad that we still get to work together in the white-ball stuff, and someone that I owe a huge amount to. I've become pretty close with over that period of time as well. So I think they're doing brilliant stuff in the white-ball teams, and I wish him all the very best in that.

Joe Root: (On whether England would approach an adventurous run chase differently under his second stint as captain) I think, again, it depends on the situation of the game, but, you always want to look to win first. I don't like the narrative of potentially being seen as a negative captain. I don't think that's how I play the game. If you watch me bat, it's certainly not how I go about things, and it's always about how can you get there? How can you get to where you want to get to at the end of it? If it's chasing the score down, how does that look? You know, can you construct a way through it? And depending on the conditions, what does that look like? So certainly we'll always look to try and win the game. But if that's not a possibility, can we sometimes find a way to get a draw?

Joe Root: (On what he learned from Ben Stokes during his time as England captain) A lot, like his playing, really. The way, I mean, he's always led from the front, whether he's a player or not. He certainly tried to do that as captain and was very successful in many ways with that. I think the clarity in terms of what was expected from the group, making sure that everyone was fully aware of what was required of them, especially at the start of his tenure, was exceptional. And, he fiercely defended his players and looked after them as best he could. He's obviously a great friend of mine, someone that we'll stay friends beyond cricket. And of course it's sad that he's no longer playing, but I think he's left a very good legacy as both a player and a leader.

Joe Root: (On whether he feels he mishandled Jofra Archer during his first stint as England captain) I think it's understanding, when you've got such an amazing talent, how to handle that. You look at the attack that we had then. We had a number of extremely high-skilled bowlers, but were all very similar. You know, Chris Woakes, Stuart Broad, Jimmy Anderson, they offered very similar attributes. And all of a sudden Jofra Archer bowls 90-mile-an-hour, he swings it in, he's got a high release point, and it's very effective and looks like a very dangerous option on flat surfaces. So I think at times maybe I did overbowl him and overuse him. But you look at the attack that we're working with this time round, it complements him really well in that respect, and there are other people that can potentially play a role that I might have used Jofra for in the past.

Joe Root: (On whether he agrees that curfews can be a sign of management losing control) I wouldn't necessarily say that. I just, that's where it sits with me. I think we have an opportunity to look after that well now and to, conduct ourselves in a way that respects that, understands it, and, I don't want people to feel like they can't enjoy winning a Test match. If they want to have a beer or, you know, at the right time go and let their hair down, then that's absolutely fine. We're human beings at the end of the day. You know what your responsibilities are. You know how you need to prepare for a Test match and what it takes, and the effects that these things can have on you. So be smart, be sensible, and just be an adult about it.

Joe Root: (Asked what success in his second stint as England captain would look like and whether he has set a time frame) I haven't put a time on it. I don't think that's necessarily the right thing to do. I think you're always looking at a potential end, or are you going to get there, or whatever? So that's never the way I've looked at anything. You know, I've never been one for having something to aim for, runs-wise as a batter, or an amount of games to play, or anything like that. So the success I see is an evolution of this team and, as I say, taking what I think there are so many good things and so many good elements to what we've already got, and making small adjustments that can make big differences. All round, there's a lot to be excited about, but in particular that seam attack. I can't wait to see them go and do their business. There's a lot to be excited about there, and it could be a serious force to be reckoned with if we get things right in the next little while.

Joe Root: (Asked whether the 2027 Ashes and the chance to become an Ashes-winning captain was a motivation) I feel like, having known you for so long, and you knowing me for so long, you've not really grasped my personality. Those personal things are not really a massive motivator for me. I think it's the collective things and what you could achieve as a group. They're the things that spur me on. And at 35, actually now, they're the drivers now that really keep me going: the fact you can have a lasting impact on a group of players, help build something, and set something up long term. It has sustainability and consistency. That's what I want to achieve from this, to really see us grow as a group of players and become our potential more than anything. (Asked what he would say if Ben Stokes texted him about the Ashes in a year's time) Oh, I don't know. Well, let's get there first.
